Sample topic
The Impact of Urban Green Spaces on Community Well-Being

In this project, I will explore how urban green spaces, such as parks and community gardens, contribute to the overall well-being of city residents (Jennings et al., 2024). I plan to investigate the psychological and physical health benefits associated with access to these green areas, including reduced stress levels, increased physical activity, and improved social cohesion among community members (Lampert et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2025). By analyzing peer-reviewed studies and case examples from cities that have successfully integrated green spaces into their urban planning, I aim to demonstrate the importance of prioritizing green infrastructure in sustainable city development. This topic not only highlights the environmental aspect of sustainability but also emphasizes its social implications, making it a compelling area of research.

Introduction · A Short History of Fossil Fuels

From Wood to Fossil Fuels: Dense, Reliable Energy

For most of history, people burned wood and relied on muscle, wind and water. Coal, then oil and natural gas, took over because they pack far more energy into every pound and can be stored, shipped and burned whenever they are needed.

How the United States switched fuels click a title
1875
1900
1925
1975
2000
Why they won dense and reliable

Dense. A pound of gasoline holds about 5.4 kWh, three times seasoned firewood (1.85 kWh); house coal holds about twice as much. Less to haul, store and carry.

Reliable. Fossil fuels are stored energy: piled, piped or pumped into a tank, then burned at any hour, in any season, far from where they were found. A waterwheel needs a river; a windmill needs wind.

U.S. EIA, Monthly Energy Review Tables D1, 1.3 and 10.1, and “The 250-year history of U.S. energy consumption” (2026). Lower heating values: Forest Research (UK) for seasoned firewood (14.7 MJ/kg) and house coal (27–31 MJ/kg); U.S. EPA, 33.7 kWh per gallon of gasoline.

13.1 · What Are Fossil Fuels?

Ancient Sunlight, Buried

The original source of all fossil fuel energy is the sun.

Where the energy comes from
Captured

Plants and plankton stored the Sun’s energy in their carbon through photosynthesis.

Buried

Covered before they could rot, their remains were pressed and heated for millions of years.

Released

Burning them gives back that ancient sunlight as heat, and their carbon as CO₂.

80% of our energy

Nearly 80% of all energy powering modern lifestyles comes from fossil fuels.

Textbook; fossil fuels were 82% of U.S. energy in 2025 (EIA).
Coal: ancient swamps turned to stone
What

A black or brown rock made mostly of carbon. The U.S. holds about 22% of the world’s reserves.

Origin

Swamp forests, much of them 359 to 299 million years ago. Deeper and hotter means more carbon: lignite 25–35%, anthracite 86–97%.

Use

About 90% of U.S. coal is burned in power plants to make electricity.

14 tons every second

burned in the United States (452 million tons in 2025).

EIA, Coal explained; Monthly Energy Review.
Natural gas: mostly methane
What

Oil and gas are hydrocarbons, which are materials made of strands of hydrogen and carbon molecules. Gas is mostly methane, CH₄.

Origin

Microscopic sea life buried deepest and hottest, above about 150 °C, breaks down into gas.

Use

The top source of U.S. electricity since 2016. 39% goes to power plants, 32% to industry, 25% to heating.

1.06 million cubic feet a second

burned in the United States: a cube 102 feet on each side.

EIA, Monthly Energy Review (2025).
Petroleum: oil from ancient seas
What

A liquid hydrocarbon from ancient microscopic organisms. The world’s most consumed fuel.

Origin

Plankton buried in oxygen-poor mud, heated to 65–150 °C (the oil window), rises until a cap rock traps it.

Use

Petroleum supplies 37% of U.S. energy; about 70% of it moves people and goods.

240 barrels every second

used in the United States (20.7 million barrels a day in 2025).

EIA, Monthly Energy Review (2025).

Dukes (2003), “Burning buried sunshine,” Climatic Change 61: 31–44; EIA, Coal explained, Natural gas explained, Today in Energy and Monthly Energy Review (2025 data); Wyoming State Geological Survey, How are oil and gas formed? Depths, temperatures and times in the animations are illustrative.

13.3 · Government Actions and the Rise of Fossil Fuels

Policy as a Driver of Energy Dominance

  • Governments have always shaped energy adoption, through regulation of competing sources, subsidies, public infrastructure, and research funding.
  • England banned wood fuel and subsidized coal in the 1500s, creating a guaranteed market. Tax structures and highway systems later enabled automobile and oil dominance.
  • Coal became the main heating fuel in England in the early 1600s, but it took 300 years for it to surpass wood as a dominant energy source.
  • Today, some governments subsidize fossil fuels, effectively lowering their market price and slowing the transition to alternatives.

13.4 · Oil: Reserves, Extraction, and Impact

Why the “number of years” changes:

Variables: use rate, technology, price per barrel.

  1. R/P
    Years left = reserves ÷ use

    In 2020 the world had about 1,732 billion barrels of proved reserves and used about 33 billion a year: about 53 years’ worth.

    BP Statistical Review (2021); Energy Institute via Our World in Data.
  2. Use
    Use rate

    Burn faster and the years shrink. World oil use passed 100 million barrels a day in 2023.

    Energy Institute, Statistical Review (2024).
  3. Tech
    Technology

    Wells recover only about 20 to 40% of the oil in a reservoir. Better drilling, fracking and enhanced recovery turn more of it into reserves.

    Muggeridge et al. (2014), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A.
  4. Price
    Price per barrel

    Reserves count only oil worth producing at today’s prices. When prices rise, costly oil, such as Canada’s oil sands, becomes a reserve.

    EIA: proved reserves are recoverable “under existing economic and operating conditions.”
  5. The paradox world proved oil reserves
    ReservesUse per yearYears left
    1980683 billion bbl24 billion29
    20201,732 billion bbl33 billion53

    Between 1980 and 2020 the world burned about 1,178 billion barrels, more than all of 1980’s reserves, and still had more left.

BP Statistical Review of World Energy (2021), proved reserves 1980–2020; Energy Institute Statistical Review via Our World in Data, oil use (converted at 2023 = 100.2 million barrels/day); Muggeridge et al. (2014); Campbell & Laherrère (1998), Scientific American; EIA glossary. “Years left” is a snapshot ratio, not a forecast.

13.4 · Natural Gas

The Fastest-Growing Fossil Fuel

Advantages
Releases 30% less CO₂ than oil and 50% less than coal per unit of energy (textbook). Surpassed coal for US electricity in 2015.
Disadvantages
Pipelines can leak methane, 25× more potent than CO₂ as a GHG. Fracking expansion raises groundwater risks.
Scale
Fracking has dramatically expanded unconventional gas supply since 2007, reshaping global energy markets.

13.4 · Hydraulic Fracturing (Fracking)

Unlocking Unconventional Reserves

  1. Process
    How it works

    A well is drilled vertically then horizontally. High-pressure water, sand, and chemicals fracture the rock; sand holds fractures open while oil or gas flows out.

    Marcellus shale lies 5,000–9,000 ft down (USGS); new Permian laterals averaged 10,867 ft in 2025 (EIA).
  2. Why
    Why it matters

    Fracking has increased the amount of natural gas that can be profitably extracted from unconventional reserves.

    Fractured wells: under 7% of U.S. gas production in 2000, about two-thirds by 2015 (EIA).
  3. Water
    Groundwater risk

    Groundwater contamination risks from fracking fluids remain a major ongoing debate.

    EPA (2016): impacts “under some circumstances,” such as spills, faulty casing or cement, and poorly treated wastewater.
  4. Waste
    Water use and wastewater

    Requires large volumes of water; contaminated wastewater must be safely disposed of.

    Median 5.1 million gallons per horizontal gas well in 2014 (USGS); deep wastewater injection drove Oklahoma’s earthquake surge (USGS).
  5. What is in fracking fluid? EPA analysis of about 39,000 wells
    water 88%sand 10%

    Additives are under 1% of the fluid, but a single well uses millions of gallons, so that is still thousands of gallons of chemicals.

U.S. EPA (2016), Hydraulic Fracturing for Oil and Gas: Impacts from the Hydraulic Fracturing Water Cycle on Drinking Water Resources; EPA (2015), FracFocus data analysis; USGS (Gallegos et al. 2015; Marcellus groundwater studies; induced earthquakes); EIA, Today in Energy (2016; Aug 2026).

13.1 · How Fossil Fuel Power Plants Work

From Fire to Wire: How Fossil Fuel Power Plants Work

Coal and natural gas plants are heat engines. They burn fuel to make heat, use the heat to spin a turbine, and turn the spin into electricity. Together they made about 58% of U.S. electricity in 2025.

  1. Burn
    Chemical energy becomes heat

    Coal or natural gas burns in a furnace. A coal plant burns about half a kilogram of coal (1.1 lb) for every kilowatt-hour it makes.

  2. Boil
    Heat becomes steam

    The fire heats purified water flowing through the boiler’s tubes into high-pressure steam at about 540 °C.

  3. Spin
    Steam spins a turbine and a generator

    Steam pushes rows of blades and spins a shaft 3,600 times a minute. A magnet on the shaft turns inside copper coils, driving current to the grid.

  4. Cool
    Most of the energy leaves as heat

    Spent steam is cooled back into water and reused. The leftover heat leaves through cooling towers and the stack: only about a third of coal’s energy becomes electricity.

  5. Coal vs. natural gas U.S. averages
    CoalNatural gas
    Fuel energy that becomes electricity32%45%combined cycle
    CO₂ per kWh, at the stack1.05 kg0.44 kg
    Share of U.S. electricity, 202517%41%

    Most gas plants burn the fuel twice: in a jet-engine-like gas turbine, then again as its hot exhaust makes steam for a second turbine.

U.S. EIA: Electricity Explained (how plants work; 2025 generation shares); Electric Power Annual, Tables 8.1–8.2 (heat rates; efficiency = 3,412 ÷ heat rate); FAQs on CO₂ per kWh (2023) and fuel per kWh (2022). U.S. averages.

© 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.
13.1 · How Fossil Fuel Power Plants Work

Where Does the Energy Go? Follow 100 Units of Fuel

Every step between the fuel and your lamp loses energy, mostly as heat. The losses multiply, so very little of the fuel’s energy ends up doing the job you wanted.

  1. Plant
    About two-thirds is lost at the plant

    A U.S. coal plant turns about 32 of every 100 units of fuel energy into electricity; a natural gas combined-cycle plant, about 45. The rest leaves as heat from the cooling tower and the stack.

    EIA heat rates, 2024 (see slide 8).
  2. Wires
    A little more on the wires

    About 5% of electricity is lost heating the power lines between the plant and your home.

    EIA, average for 2018–2022.
  3. Home
    Then the device decides

    A 60-watt incandescent bulb and a 9-watt LED give about the same light. The LED needs about 85% less electricity, and so about 85% less coal.

    FTC: about 800 lumens each; DOE: LEDs use at least 75% less energy.
  4. Nation
    The national picture

    In 2019, U.S. power plants used 38 quads of energy to deliver 14 quads of electricity: more than 60% was lost in conversion.

    EIA, Today in Energy (2020).
  5. Efficiencies multiply fuel needed for the same light
    IncandescentLED
    Coal plant (32%)100 units15 units
    Gas combined cycle (45%)71 units11 units

    100 × 0.32 × 0.95 = 30 units reach the outlet. Swapping the bulb saves more fuel than swapping the plant.

U.S. EIA: Electric Power Annual heat rates (2024); Today in Energy, “More than 60% of energy used for electricity generation is lost in conversion” (2020); FAQ on transmission and distribution losses (2018–2022). FTC, “Shopping for light bulbs”; U.S. DOE Energy Saver, LED lighting.

13.3 · Is ‘Clean Coal’ Clean?

The Limits of ‘Clean’ Fossil Fuels

The same coal plant, the same coal, the same electricity. Only the equipment between the boiler and the stack is different.

Some coal power plants claim to use ‘clean coal’ technology, in some cases reducing sulfur emissions.
‘Clean coal’ is largely a marketing claim rather than a description of emissions neutrality.

EPA, Documentation for the 2023 Reference Case, Ch. 5 (wet scrubber 98% SO₂ removal); EPA, Air Pollution Control Technology Fact Sheet: SCR (70–90% NOx); EPA, 2023 Power Sector Programs Progress Report (1995–2023 totals); EIA, “How much carbon dioxide is produced per kilowatthour?” (coal 2.31 lb, 2023).

13.4 · Coal: Extraction and Combustion

The Most Abundant and Most Polluting

  1. Reserves

    The US, Russia, China, and Australia hold over two-thirds of global coal reserves.

  2. Extraction

    Extraction: underground boring machines or surface blasting; mountaintop removal deposits waste in adjacent valleys, permanently altering landscapes.

  3. Water

    Acid mine drainage destroys aquatic habitat; coal mines contribute 7% of US methane emissions through venting.

  4. CO₂

    Coal emits significantly more CO₂ per unit of energy.

IPCC AR5 (2014), Working Group III, Annex III, Table A.III.2: median lifecycle emissions in grams of CO₂-equivalent per kWh, including mining, building and fuel; consistent with Klein & Whalley et al. Home: EIA, 10,791 kWh per U.S. residential customer (2022).

13.4–13.5 · Fossil Fuel Disasters and the Future of Fossil Fuels

Disasters and a Shrinking Market Share

A shrinking market share
  1. Economic Pressure

    Fossil fuels’ collective market share has been shrinking for over 100 years. As alternatives grow cheaper, the transition accelerates.

  2. Geopolitical Risk

    Finite reserves are unevenly distributed, driving competition and conflict. Energy security shapes foreign policy globally.

  3. Social Cost of Carbon

    Estimated at $51+/ton; damage to property, agriculture, and health that is currently externalized and not reflected in market prices.

Disasters: NOAA (Exxon Valdez, Deepwater Horizon); EPA (Enbridge, Martin County, Kingston); NTSB (San Bruno); California Air Resources Board (Aliso Canyon); MSHA (Upper Big Branch). Market share: U.S. EIA, Monthly Energy Review Tables 1.3 and 10.1 and Appendix D1 (1850–2025).

13.5 · The Social Cost of Carbon

Pricing the True Cost of Emissions

Social Cost of Carbon: An economic measure of the damage caused by one additional ton of GHG emissions, including harm to property, agriculture, and human health. Currently estimated at a minimum of $51 per ton.

  1. Hidden
    An externality

    This cost is currently “externalized,” borne by society rather than by producers, making fossil fuels appear cheaper than they actually are.

    Rennert et al. (2022): about $185 per tonne, mostly heat-related deaths ($90) and lost crops ($84).
  2. Price
    Internalizing it

    Internalizing the social cost through carbon taxes or cap-and-trade makes the true price visible and changes incentives.

    At $190 a tonne, each gallon of gasoline carries about $1.69 of climate damage (8.9 kg of CO₂ per gallon, EPA).
  3. Clean
    Cheaper alternatives

    Wind and solar are already reducing costs.

  4. Who sets the number? dollars per tonne of CO₂
    Discount rateValue
    U.S. interim estimate (2021)3%$51
    U.S. EPA (2023)2%$190
    Rennert et al., Nature (2022)2%$185

    In January 2025, Executive Order 14154 withdrew the federal estimates. Lower discount rates count future harm more and raise the number.

U.S. EPA (2023), Report on the Social Cost of Greenhouse Gases; Interagency Working Group (2021); Rennert et al. (2022), Nature 610:687–692; Executive Order 14154 (2025); EPA greenhouse gas equivalencies; EIA (2023). Estimates for teaching; every number here carries wide scientific and ethical uncertainty.

13.5 · Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS)

Preventing CO₂ from Reaching the Atmosphere

  1. 1

    CCS captures CO₂ before it escapes into the atmosphere, then injects it underground for long-term storage, potentially enabling lower-carbon fossil fuel use.

  2. 2

    Enhanced oil recovery (EOR): captured CO₂ is compressed and pumped underground to force additional oil from depleted wells.

  3. 3

    CCS remains expensive and energy-intensive

  4. 4

    Critics note that EOR enables continued fossil fuel extraction rather than reducing it.

Today the world captures about 50 million tonnes of CO₂ a year (IEA, 2025), about 0.1% of the 37.8 billion tonnes energy use emitted in 2024.

IEA, “Is carbon capture too expensive?” (17 February 2021): capture $15–25/t (concentrated) and $40–120/t (dilute); U.S. onshore pipeline $2–14/t; most onshore storage under $10/t. IEA CCUS Projects Database (2025); IEA Global Energy Review 2025; U.S. IRS, 45Q credit; IPCC Special Report on CCS (2005).

Chapter 13 · Key Concepts

Fossil Fuels: Energy of the Industrial Age

Hydrocarbons
Hydrogen-carbon molecules forming oil and natural gas
Proven Reserves
Resources profitably accessible at current prices and technology
Fracking
High-pressure fluid fractures rock to release oil or gas
Mountaintop Removal
Entire mountaintops removed to access underlying coal
Jevons Paradox
Efficiency gains lower resource cost, increasing consumption
Social Cost of Carbon
Economic damage from one ton of GHG, currently externalized
Cap-and-Trade
Emissions ceiling with tradeable pollution permits
Carbon Capture (CCS)
Preventing CO₂ from reaching atmosphere via underground injection
